title: Beza and Garissolius: fiducia is faith’s inseparable effect — verbal clash only
source_text: LXXIII. Neque per fiduciam aliud intelligunt Beza & Garissolius, aliique supra a nobis citati, qui cum eo docent fiduciam non esse fidei partem, sed solum effectum inseparabilem, qui cum fide quidem indivulse cohaeret, veruntamen est ab ea distinguendus. Unde patet Molinaeum, Bezam, & Garissolium reipsa consentire cum Theologis illis, qui volunt quidem fiduciam fidei praecipuam partem constituere; sed fiduciae nomine intelligunt certam illam persuasionem, qua fidelis de divina erga se gratia & benevolentia plene persuasus est, & bona in Evangelio fidelibus promissa ad se peculiariter pertinere judicat. Nam Theologi modo nominati istam quoque persuasionem pro fidei parte agnoscunt: Sed eam nolunt fiduciam dici, & hoc nomine potius designandam existimant animi tranquillitatem, libertatem, atque constantiam, quae ex tali persuasione de Dei erga nos benevolentia oritur. Et sic cum in re ipsa utrique consentiant, modo solum loquendi differunt.
pass_a_gloss: Nor do Beza and Garissolius, and others cited by us above, understand anything else by trust, who with him teach that trust is not a part of faith, but only an inseparable effect, which indeed coheres indivisibly with faith, yet is nevertheless to be distinguished from it. Whence it is plain that du Moulin, Beza, and Garissolius agree in the thing itself with those theologians who indeed want trust to constitute the chief part of faith; but by the name of trust understand that certain persuasion by which the believer is fully persuaded of divine grace and goodwill toward himself, and judges that the goods promised in the Gospel to the faithful pertain to himself peculiarly. For the theologians just named also acknowledge that persuasion as a part of faith: but they do not want it to be called trust, and by this name think rather to be designated the tranquillity, liberty, and constancy of mind which arises from such persuasion of God's goodwill toward us. And so while both sides agree in the thing itself, they differ only in the mode of speaking.
pass_b_english: Beza, Garissolius (and du Moulin with them): fiducia is not a part of faith but its inseparable effect — coheres with faith, yet is distinct from it.
Those who make fiducia faith’s chief part mean by the name that sure persuasion of God’s grace toward me and that Gospel goods are peculiarly mine.
Beza’s side grants that persuasion as part of faith, but reserves “fiducia” for the quiet, liberty, and constancy that rise from it.
Same thing; only the wording differs.
